sentences.text: Use the read tool — not shell commands like cat — to inspect text files.
Results include line numbers.
Use offset and limit to continue reading large files.
Use the grep tool — not shell grep or rg — to search file contents.
Returns matching lines with line numbers, grouped by file.
Use read on a matched file when you need surrounding context.
Use the glob tool — not shell find — to discover files by path pattern.
Results are files only, never directories.
A pattern with no separator matches basenames at any depth.
Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents.
Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first.
Prefer edit for targeted changes.
Use edit for targeted changes to an existing UTF-8 text file.
It replaces literal old_string with new_string; old_string must appear exactly once unless replace_all is set.
Read the file first unless you just created or edited it in this session.
Execute a PowerShell command (pwsh -Command) and return its stdout/stderr.
Each call runs in a fresh pwsh process: no cwd, variables or functions persist between calls — pass workdir instead of using cd.
Non-zero exits are reported as [exit code: N] markers.
Not for reading or searching files — use read/grep/glob.
Execute a bash command and return its stdout/stderr.
Each call runs in a fresh process: no state persists between calls.
Not for reading or searching files — use read/grep/glob.
Read a background job by the job id returned by the tool that started it.
Reads are non-blocking unless wait is true.
Do not busy-poll or sleep on a job.
Delegate a self-contained task to a subagent working in its own context.
Give it a complete standalone prompt: it does not see this conversation.
The subagent returns its result, not its intermediate steps.
Search the web for current information.
Returns an optional summary answer and a list of source URLs.
Cite the relevant URLs as markdown links.
